history: Credit is trust, and the word says so. Latin credere meant ‘to believe, to trust’, and creditum, its past participle used as a noun, was a loan: something you gave a person because you trusted them to give it back. Italian credito keeps that sense in banking: una carta di credito, un credito d'imposta, a tax credit. It also means recognition for what someone has done, as in dare credito, ‘to believe someone’ and not ‘to lend’. The family is large. Credere is ‘to believe’, la credenza is ‘a belief’, and un creditore is the person you owe money to. The opposite is debito, from Latin debere, ‘to owe’. Whether credere itself is built from ‘to put one's heart’ is a scholarly hypothesis.
historyEinfach: Credito comes from Latin credere, ‘to trust’. A creditum was a loan, because you trust the person to pay it back. Today credito is used for bank credit, a tax credit, and also for trust: dare credito means ‘to believe someone’. The opposite of credito is debito.
